title: Anchor Ice
description:
A game about sliding becoming difficult because movable objects determine where movement can stop.

The agent slides across ice until blocked. Crates also slide when pushed, but a crate that enters a visible anchor socket nests into it and becomes a permanent stopper. The player creates stopping points, uses them to reach new pushing angles, and must avoid anchoring a crate before its final useful position.

## Game idea

This is a compact, top-down ice puzzle about arranging the surfaces that make precise movement possible. The primary objective is to make the agent come to rest on a clearly marked exit pad; merely sliding across the exit does not complete the level, so the required final stopping point remains visually explicit.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` launch the agent in the chosen direction. The agent continues until meeting a wall, an anchored crate, or a crate it cannot push. When it contacts a pushable crate with clear ice beyond it, the crate slides in that direction until obstructed or caught by an anchor socket, while the agent settles in the crate’s vacated cell. A blocked direction produces a brief bump and visible ice-scrape without changing the settled state.

The board contains only ice, walls, the agent, sliding crates, recessed anchor sockets, and the exit. Ordinary crates sit visibly above the ice and remain movable; a socket resembles an open floor clamp, and a captured crate is shown lowered into it with closed clamps, making its permanent status unmistakable. Both loose and anchored crates block movement, but only loose crates can be pushed. A moving crate stops immediately when it enters a socket, even if open ice continues beyond it.

Because every move ends in a stable grid arrangement, the current frame shows all relevant information: positions, which crates remain usable, which sockets are occupied, and whether the agent has a viable line toward the exit. Early puzzles avoid punishing premature captures; later ones make dangerous sockets conspicuous and provide enough open structure for players to test sliding and collision behavior before committing.

## Strategic discoveries

- **Crates are movable brakes:** A crate aligned with an inaccessible lane visibly offers the agent somewhere to stop, and pushing it leaves the agent at its former position. Progress can require approaching a crate not to relocate it toward a socket, but to gain the exact stopping square needed for a perpendicular route.

- **Crates position one another:** A sliding crate visibly halts against another crate rather than passing through it. Players can therefore use one loose crate as a backstop to place another at a useful intermediate location, then rearrange or push the backstop afterward.

- **Anchoring changes function:** The open clamp and permanently seated result make it clear that anchoring trades mobility for reliability. A crate may need to serve several temporary braking or collision roles before being committed as the fixed stopper that opens the final route.

- **Anchors become construction supports:** Once fixed, an anchored crate can stop both the agent and later sliding crates from multiple directions. Later puzzles require choosing which socket to fill first so that the resulting stopper enables precise placement of the remaining crate rather than merely shortening a path.

## Broad progression

Foundational scenes establish uninterrupted sliding, pushing, socket capture, and the need to stop on the exit. Early composition makes movable-crate braking and perpendicular access necessary. The middle phase reuses crate-on-crate stopping in both agent-routing and crate-placement contexts. Late puzzles combine temporary crate roles with carefully timed permanent anchoring, without adding new devices. The final phase asks the player to construct a chain of useful stopping points whose order preserves every required pushing angle.

title: Conveyor Weave
description:
A game about conveyor travel becoming difficult because the player must configure the route before entering it.

Stepping onto a conveyor carries the agent along its arrows. Visibly rotatable conveyor cells cycle through four directions, while one-way gates accept movement only from their indicated side. Rotation persists, so configuring one journey may destroy the route needed for the return journey.

The game is a compact top-down routing puzzle whose primary objective is to bring the agent onto a clearly marked exit pad. Ordinary floor forms preparation areas and small landings around conveyor passages. Some routes lead away from the exit to positions needed for reconfiguration, making a later return across shared belts part of the same objective rather than a separate task.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the agent one cell and set its visibly marked facing direction. While the agent stands on ordinary floor, `SPACE` turns the faced adjacent rotatable conveyor clockwise; its circular rim distinguishes it from fixed conveyor cells. An ineligible `SPACE` press pulses the faced edge with a lock symbol, while blocked directional movement produces a brief bump against the obstruction.

Entering a conveyor begins automatic travel along its arrows. Travel continues through connected conveyor cells until the agent reaches ordinary floor or the next forced movement is blocked by a wall, a conflicting conveyor edge, or the forbidden side of a one-way gate. In a blockage, the agent remains visibly stopped on the conveyor cell that attempted the move; there is no rewind or hidden journey state. From this settled position, directional input can step onto any adjacent ordinary floor, and puzzle geometry ensures every possible blocked endpoint has at least one such local escape.

Conveyor arrows remain fully visible beneath the agent. A blocked edge flashes red and then retains a small jam mark while occupied, so the cause and available recovery can be read from the current frame. One-way gates are bold barriers between cells with an entry chevron on their permitted side. Rotation is allowed only from ordinary floor, so even after escaping a jam the player must stand in the right place to prepare the next trip.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Trace backward from a landing.** A forward-looking route can visibly end at a wall or barred gate, while the landing’s approach edge identifies the final required arrow; this backward reasoning becomes necessary when several branches initially look viable.

- **Approach determines passage.** A nearby gate may reject the most direct route because its chevron faces the other way, revealing why a longer weave that reaches the same gate from another side is useful and reusable.

- **A jam can reveal a staging shore.** When an obvious configuration stops beside ordinary floor, the local escape exposes that floor as a new position from which adjacent belts can be rotated; later puzzles require intentionally routing to such a shore without adding a new rule.

- **Schedule shared belts by access.** Outward and return journeys may need opposite orientations on the same conveyor, and visible adjacency from the far landing shows which shared cells can be changed after crossing and which must already be reserved for the return.

Foundational scenes establish floor movement, clockwise rotation, automatic travel, local jams, and gate markings in clean isolation. Early compositions require complete route tracing and correct gate approach. Middle puzzles turn landings and safe jam shores into configuration positions with different reach. Late puzzles combine those access differences with belts shared by outward and return routes. The final phase demands a coherent weave in which each persistent rotation supports the journey that must happen before it is changed again.

title: Corner Rails
description:
A game about following rails becoming difficult because the agent must steer both itself and a cargo cart through the same network.

The agent and cart travel only along visible rails. The agent can rotate adjacent junction pieces, changing how later arrivals are deflected. The cart moves along the rails when pushed and must reach its terminal, often before the agent can use the same junction configuration to reach the exit.

## Game Idea

A compact grid contains fixed rail segments, rotatable corner junctions, one agent, one cargo cart, a cart terminal, and an agent exit. Rail connections are drawn continuously across cell edges, and each corner junction prominently displays its current L-shaped route. The terminal bears a cart silhouette; the exit bears an agent silhouette and remains visibly shut until the cart is docked.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the agent to an adjacent cell when the rails connect and set its visibly marked facing direction. Moving toward the cart pushes it one rail cell; when the cart enters or occupies a corner, the corner’s visible bend determines its route. `SPACE` turns the faced adjacent rotatable junction clockwise. Eligible junctions receive a clear outline, making the affected piece unmistakable before the action.

Neither occupant can leave the rails or pass through the other. A move fails if rail ends do not meet, the destination is blocked, or the cart has no connected cell into which it can advance. The conflicting rail ends briefly flash without changing state. An occupied junction cannot rotate and visibly rattles when targeted with `SPACE`, preventing reconfiguration beneath the agent or cart.

The cart can only be pushed, never pulled. Each successful push leaves the agent in the cart’s former cell. When the cart reaches its terminal, it locks there; the terminal glows and the exit opens, leaving the agent to route itself to the exit using the remaining accessible junctions. Every settled frame shows junction orientations, occupancy, docking state, and whether the exit is open.

## Strategic Discoveries

- **Configure before committing.** A cart approaching several corners may occupy or cut off junctions after the first push, while adjacency outlines reveal which pieces can currently be reached. Later situations require preparing multiple bends from different sides before advancing the cart.

- **Exploit bidirectional bends.** The same corner orientation that sends the cart toward its terminal can provide a useful route for the agent approaching from the opposite arm. Continuous rail lines make this testable when treating the two routes independently creates a visible impasse.

- **Push to reposition the agent.** Because a push moves the agent into the cart’s former cell, sending the cart through a bend can carry the agent onto a branch unreachable by ordinary walking. This becomes necessary for reaching the side of a junction from which it can be rotated.

- **Clear shared rail by docking.** A cart occupying a junction or access rail may need to be advanced fully to its terminal before the agent can reconfigure the route to the exit. The obstruction and newly exposed track make this ordering consequence concrete and reusable.

## Progression

Foundational scenes separately establish connected movement, visible corner rotation, pushing, docking, and the opened exit, with forgiving routes for experimentation. Early composition requires orienting corners before pushing and recognizing that agent and cart share the same physical connections. Middle puzzles contrast advance preparation with using pushes to reposition the agent. Late puzzles combine inaccessible junction sides, bidirectional use, and carts occupying critical rail cells without adding unrelated devices. The final phase makes the cart route, the agent’s position after each push, and the post-docking exit route depend on the same small set of corners.

title: Turnback Gates
description:
A game about crossing one-way gates becoming difficult because every crossing reverses the gate.

Each gate visibly points toward its currently permitted entry direction. Passing through flips the arrow. The agent must reach an object and then escape with it, so every inward crossing changes the route available for the outward journey.

**Game idea**

The agent begins on a clearly marked start tile inside a compact walled structure. A relic rests elsewhere, and a boundary escape arch occupies a third, distinct location. The objective is solely to collect the relic and carry it through that arch: exactly retracing the inward journey returns the agent to the start, not to the exit.

Turnback gates span passages between adjacent floor cells. Each gate’s large arrow points toward the side from which entry is currently permitted. Approaching from that side crosses the gate and reverses its arrow; approaching from the other side leaves the agent in place, with a barred flash and bump that make the failed direction clear. Because a successful crossing makes the gate point toward the agent’s new side, every crossing can immediately be reversed.

Controls are only `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT`, moving one orthogonal cell. Contact automatically crosses a permissive gate, collects the relic, or exits when carrying it. The relic vanishes from its pedestal and appears prominently on the agent when collected, while the arch changes from a closed relic-emblem frame to an unmistakably open exit.

Walls, gates, arrows, agent, pedestal, relic, start, and arch remain visually distinct. The settled board exposes every gate orientation and whether the relic is carried; there are no timers or move limits. Following any traversed route backward restores its gates, so experimentation remains safely reversible even when a chosen route fails to lead toward the separate escape.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Reversible probing:** Crossing back through a just-used gate restores both the earlier side and arrow, visibly demonstrating that branches can be inspected without permanently disturbing them. This makes early experiments safe and later lets the player compare routes before committing to relic collection.

- **Prepare from the far side:** To permit a future crossing from one side, the player can first reach the opposite side by a loop and cross backward through the gate. The resulting arrow visibly faces the desired approach, making this necessary for staging a gate that will later carry the relic toward the arch.

- **Rehearse the escape backward:** Traveling from the arch-side region toward the relic can orient an entire chain of gates for the eventual journey in the opposite direction. Later puzzles reuse this consequence at branching routes, where only one backward traversal prepares a continuous escape path.

- **The last crossing decides:** A prepared gate is reversed again if used for some intervening journey, so shared access-and-escape passages must receive their useful orientation on their final pre-relic crossing. The constantly visible arrows reveal when an otherwise sensible preparation has been overwritten and make ordering, rather than memory, the challenge.

**Broad progression**

Foundational scenes establish permitted entry, reversal, immediate retreat, relic collection, and the separate escape location using generous loops. Early composition requires approaching a blocked gate from its indicated side to prepare it for later travel. The middle phase turns backward rehearsal into a reusable method, then contrasts it with routes whose gates are disturbed by reaching the relic. Late puzzles combine shared passages, loops, and competing preparations without adding another rule family. The final phase asks the player to shape a complete relic-to-arch route while approaching the relic from the distinct start.

title: Color Ferry
description:
A game about color-locked routes becoming difficult because the agent can transport only one usable color at a time.

The agent can carry one pigment stone. While carried, its color is displayed on the agent and determines which colored gates are passable. Touching a dye basin transfers that basin’s color to the stone, allowing one physical object to act as several different keys—but only in a carefully planned order.

## Expanded game idea

The player guides an agent carrying a single pigment stone through compact, walled routes toward a clearly marked ferry dock. Reaching the dock is the sole victory condition. The stone remains carried throughout a level, so the puzzle concerns transporting and repeatedly recoloring that one object rather than managing an inventory.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the agent one grid cell. Entering a dye-basin cell immediately recolors the carried stone; basins remain full and may be reused. No other control is active.

The stone is large and prominently mounted on the agent. Each color also has a distinct stripe or symbol shared by its basins and gates, ensuring that color relationships remain readable. Gates matching the stone are visibly raised or retracted, while every other gate remains visibly barred; thus the settled frame directly shows both the current color and which passages are usable. A blocked movement makes the struck gate give a brief mismatch pulse while remaining closed.

Basins are shallow floor features that the agent can walk across, making recoloring a concrete spatial commitment. Changing color immediately closes the previously matching gates and opens the newly matching ones. Walls shape the routes, while the ferry dock uses a persistent agent-and-stone emblem to communicate the destination without adding another requirement.

### Strategic discoveries

- **Finish before repainting:** A tempting nearby basin can close gates that were just opened, visibly cutting off unfinished branches. Later puzzles require completing everything needed on one side of a color gate before surrendering that color.

- **Treat basins as transfer stations:** A basin beyond one colored gate can be entered using the old color and departed using its new color. The visible gate swap reveals how a basin can connect two otherwise incompatible route segments, and later chains require several such transfers.

- **Cycle colors instead of seeking new keys:** Because used basins remain visibly full, the same color can be recovered after an intervening recolor. Alternating sequences such as one color, another, then the first again make revisiting a known basin necessary in contrasting parts of the route.

- **Skirt a useful basin until the right moment:** Stepping on every accessible basin greedily can overwrite a color needed for the next gate. Open floor around some basins provides a safe experiment showing that bypassing and approaching later is part of route planning, not an unexplained exception.

### Broad progression

Foundational scenes establish movement, matching gates, automatic recoloring, and the ferry destination in safe routes where choices remain recoverable. Early composition makes the closing of the previous color’s gates matter and introduces reusable basins. The middle phase contrasts optional basins with mandatory transfer points and requires deliberate color cycling. Late puzzles combine alternate approaches to the same basin with several gates reacting simultaneously, without introducing new devices. The final phase asks the player to plan a complete ferry route whose geometric direction and required color order repeatedly diverge.

title: Bridge Stock
description:
A game about crossing gaps becoming difficult because every bridge consumes a piece that may be needed elsewhere.

Planks can be carried and placed across marked one-cell gaps. Once installed, a plank locks into the gap and becomes ordinary walkable terrain. Later levels require using limited planks to enter regions, preserve return routes, and avoid permanently bridging the wrong crossing.

**Game idea**

Bridge Stock is a compact, top-down grid puzzle about allocating a visible supply of wooden planks while navigating toward a clearly marked exit. The board contains ordinary floor, walls, impassable open void, marked one-cell gaps with obvious bridge sockets, loose planks, installed bridges, the player, and the exit. All relevant areas and loose planks remain visible, so success depends on reasoning rather than searching or remembering hidden information.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move one cell. Walking onto a loose plank collects it, adding a distinct plank icon to the carried bundle beside the player; attempting to move into a marked gap while carrying at least one plank consumes one, installs it, and moves the player onto the resulting bridge. Installed planks retain their wooden appearance but thereafter behave exactly like floor.

An unbridged gap blocks movement when the bundle is empty: its sockets flash and the empty bundle visibly shakes. Walls give a short bump, while unmarked void has no sockets and can never receive a plank, clearly separating resource failure from invalid terrain. Stepping onto the exit wins; there are no secondary completion conditions.

Because bridges cannot be recovered, every placement permanently changes both the traversable board and the remaining stock. Early situations avoid fatal choices, allowing the player to test collection, installation, and free recrossing safely. Later failures remain visually explainable: an unused crossing stands ahead, the bundle is empty, and every spent plank remains visible in the specific gap that consumed it.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Spend to gain:** A gap may guard several visible loose planks, revealing that paying one plank can produce a larger usable stock. This becomes necessary when profitable regions must be opened before crossings that only consume resources.

- **Permanent access:** The installed plank’s persistent presence shows that its cost is paid only once, even if the route is crossed repeatedly. A carefully chosen bridge can therefore provide both entry and a dependable return route, while a nearby alternative may be redundant.

- **Reject the tempting shortcut:** A short gap-crossing can compete with a longer existing floor route, and the spent plank remains visibly stranded in that shortcut. Later puzzles require recognizing when walking farther preserves stock for an unavoidable crossing elsewhere.

- **Budget to the next supply:** Several consecutive visible gaps can exhaust the bundle before the next group of planks is reached. Players must count concrete carried pieces, compare route costs, and sometimes visit a replenishing side region before committing to the apparent direct route.

**Progression**

Foundational scenes establish collecting planks, automatic installation, permanent bridges, and the exit objective without dangerous ambiguity. Early composition introduces crossings that differ in visible cost and reward, making spend-to-gain and shortcut avoidance necessary. The middle phase reuses permanent access through branching regions where one bridge can support several later journeys. Late puzzles combine replenishing regions, optional crossings, and required gap chains while adding no new object family. The final phase demands a coherent ordering of region entry, stock growth, return access, and final bridge expenditure.

title: Towline
description:
A game about pulling cargo becoming difficult because unsupported cargo immediately falls.

The agent can attach to and pull a heavy block. After every action, unsupported blocks fall vertically until landing. The player must pull cargo across ledges, use temporary supports, and sometimes descend alongside it without letting it fall into an unrecoverable shaft before reaching its dock.

Towline is a deterministic side-view grid puzzle. The player controls a small hovering tug that can travel through open cells around solid terrain and cargo; gravity affects cargo, not the tug. Each cargo block is a large, clearly weighted crate, while docks are recessed, crate-sized bays whose outline fills and glows while occupied. A level is complete when every cargo block rests in a dock.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the tug one cell. `SPACE` attaches a towline to a horizontally adjacent cargo block or detaches the current line. While attached, moving directly away from the block pulls it horizontally into the tug’s former cell; incompatible movement strains the visible line but does not move anything. The persistent line makes attachment state unmistakable, and blocked movement produces a brief shake at the obstruction.

After every successful move, pull, attachment, or detachment, every cargo block lacking solid terrain or another cargo block directly beneath it falls straight down until supported. The destination column is always visible before acting; falling has no hidden variation. Early areas place floors beneath experiments, while later shafts are visibly deep or bottomless, clearly warning that a poorly placed drop may require an external reset.

Cargo blocks are also the game’s only movable supports. A crate dropped into a gap can create a temporary landing surface or extend a ledge for another crate, but it remains cargo that must eventually be extracted and delivered. Because the tug pulls rather than pushes, the player must also preserve open space on the side from which a desired pull will be made.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Falling as controlled transport:** A crate need not remain at its starting height; visible lower ledges reveal that pulling it past an edge can place it safely below. This becomes necessary when the tug must descend, circle around, and resume towing from a new side.

- **Cargo supports cargo:** A crate visibly stops atop another crate, revealing that one delivery can temporarily become flooring for the next. Later puzzles reuse this both to span gaps and to create an intermediate landing height above a dangerous shaft.

- **Choose the drop column before release:** Since falling is immediate and vertical, the final horizontal pull before an edge determines the entire descent. Narrow docks and offset lower ledges make careful alignment necessary without introducing another rule.

- **Recover supports in the right geometric order:** A lower crate cannot be pulled while another rests on it, and the required pulling side may become inaccessible after a drop. The visible stack and surrounding airspace expose the impasse, encouraging the player to move the upper cargo onward before reclaiming its support.

Foundational scenes teach attachment, horizontal pulling, and immediate settling over forgiving floors. Early composition requires deliberate edge drops and repositioning the tug at a lower height. The middle phase introduces multiple cargo blocks so their existing ability to support one another becomes necessary in contrasting gap and stacking situations. Late puzzles combine support order, tug access, and hazardous drop columns without adding unrelated devices. The final phase asks the player to construct and dismantle a route from the same cargo that must ultimately occupy the docks.

title: One-Hand Courier
description:
A game about carrying keys becoming difficult because the final objective occupies the same hand.

The agent can carry exactly one object. Carried symbols permit passage through matching gates, while inserting them into visible sockets activates local mechanisms. The final object must also be carried to the exit, forcing the player to stage keys, reopen routes, and decide where each item must be left before collecting the objective.

**Game idea**

A top-down grid puzzle follows a courier moving among loose symbol keys, matching barred gates, floor sockets, a single parcel, and the parcel-shaped exit. The foundational objective is always visible: pick up the parcel and enter the exit while still carrying it.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the courier. `SPACE` picks up a loose object beneath the courier when their hand is empty, drops the carried object on an ordinary free cell, inserts a matching carried key when standing on a socket, or retrieves that key from the socket with an empty hand. The carried object is shown prominently above the courier, while an empty-hand icon makes capacity immediately readable.

A closed gate bears the same large shape and color marking as its key. Attempting to move through while carrying that key briefly retracts the gate and completes the move; it closes again afterward. Each socket is visibly connected to one nearby gate and carries the same symbol: inserting its key holds that gate open until the key is retrieved. Thus a key can serve either as portable permission or as a stationary latch, never both simultaneously.

The parcel can be picked up, dropped, and staged like a key, but matches no gate or socket. The exit displays a parcel silhouette and only completes the puzzle when the courier enters carrying it. Wrong keys remain in hand when offered to a socket, mismatched gates rattle and flash their required symbol, and invalid drops visibly bounce back, ensuring failed actions are informative rather than silent. All keys remain recoverable, and open gates, occupied sockets, loose objects, and the courier’s hand are fully readable in every settled frame.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Turn permission into infrastructure:** A carried key opens only its own passage, but placing it in the gate’s socket leaves the route open for a different object. The visibly occupied socket and retracted gate suggest this conversion, which becomes necessary when transporting another key or the parcel.

- **Stage before reclaiming:** An object can be carried through a latched gate and left on the far side before the latch key is removed. Seeing both objects safely beyond the threshold reveals how one key can close a finished route behind the courier and later serve elsewhere.

- **Choose the key’s final side:** Because retrieving a socketed key closes its gate, the courier must arrange themself and all needed cargo on the useful side first. Later puzzles reuse this consequence at junctions where the same symbol key can support different gates, but only in a viable order.

- **Prepare a parcel-only route:** Picking up the parcel removes all handheld gate permissions, so every unavoidable gate on the remaining route must already be latched open. The parcel’s lack of a symbol makes this constraint visible and turns collecting it into the culmination of earlier staging rather than an extra rule.

Foundational scenes establish carrying capacity, matching passage, and socket latching separately in recoverable spaces. Early composition requires opening a route for a differently marked key, then staging cargo before reclaiming a latch. Middle puzzles reuse those consequences across branches and repeated symbols, making the side on which each loose object is left matter. Late puzzles combine key reuse, gate closure, and parcel staging without introducing unrelated devices. The final phase asks the player to transform a temporarily navigable network into one traversable with the parcel occupying the only hand.

title: Exchange Rooms
description:
A game about swapping places becoming difficult because every swap also exchanges access properties.

The agent swaps positions with an adjacent colored statue. The agent and statue also exchange their visible colors, changing which gates the agent can cross and which goal accepts each statue. The level ends only when all statues simultaneously occupy matching pads.

The game takes place in compact tiled rooms. The agent, every statue, each gate, and each pad displays a bold color-and-pattern emblem, allowing properties to remain distinguishable without relying on hue alone. Pads remain visible as outlined floor insets beneath occupants; a correctly matched statue gains a persistent bright border, so every part of the win condition can be inspected directly.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the agent one cell. Moving toward an adjacent statue performs the swap: the agent enters the statue’s cell, the statue enters the agent’s former cell, and their emblems exchange. Moving into a mismatched gate, wall, or otherwise blocked cell produces a clear bump and briefly brightens the obstruction.

Only the agent can traverse gates, and only while its current emblem matches the gate. Statues remain on ordinary floor and pads; swaps cannot place them into walls or gate cells. Because a statue always lands where the agent was standing, moving one requires reaching the side toward which it should travel. Repeating an unobstructed swap in the opposite direction restores both positions and colors, making early experimentation safely reversible.

A pad accepts whichever statue currently bears its emblem, regardless of that statue’s original color. Thus color is not permanent identity but a visible, transferable access property. All colors already present among the agent and statues are conserved and merely permuted, making every apparent recoloring understandable from the settled frame.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Stand on the destination:** A statue moves into the agent’s former cell, visibly revealing that the agent must first occupy a pad or other desired destination. Later rooms require approaching the same statue from different sides to route it through constrained spaces.

- **Deliver the pad’s color:** The statue receives the agent’s previous emblem, so standing on a pad with that pad’s color before swapping can solve placement and matching in one action. Incorrectly colored statues on correctly located pads visibly demonstrate why position alone is insufficient.

- **Carry colors between statues:** Swapping with a statue lets the agent take its emblem through matching gates or onward to another statue, while leaving the agent’s old emblem behind. This makes statues both cargo and color sources, and forces useful chains of exchanges rather than independent solutions.

- **Plan color cycles:** Since exchanges only permute visible emblems, fixing one statue may transfer its unwanted color into the agent rather than eliminate it. Later puzzles make that displaced color visibly necessary elsewhere, encouraging cyclic assignments that finish several pads together.

**Progression:** Foundational rooms separately establish movement, destination-side swapping, emblem exchange, matching pads, and gates with generous space for reversal. Early composition makes the player combine correct approach direction with carrying the required pad color. Middle rooms reuse color carrying across gates and statue routing in contrasting room shapes. Late rooms intertwine access and placement, so an emblem needed beyond a gate must be obtained without stranding the statue that currently holds it. The final phase demands one coherent cycle of positional swaps and color transfers that leaves every pad glowing simultaneously.

title: Stone Skaters
description:
A game about pushing stones becoming difficult because each stone slides until something stops it.

The agent moves normally, but pushed stones slide across smooth floor. Goal sockets capture compatible stones and become solid obstacles, so delivered stones can serve as new stopping surfaces for later deliveries. Ordering determines which final positions remain reachable.

**Game idea.** A compact, top-down grid shows smooth floor, fixed walls, the agent, loose round stones, and recessed goal sockets. Stones and sockets carry large matching symbols or colors; these markings remain visible even when a stone is near or over the wrong socket. An empty socket looks flat and traversable, while a correctly filled socket visibly clamps around its stone and rises into a solid, immovable obstacle. The sole objective is to fill every socket with a compatible stone, with each unfilled socket remaining an obvious visible requirement.

**Controls and rules.** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the agent one cell. Moving into a loose stone pushes it in that direction; the stone then slides in a straight line until a wall, another loose stone, or a captured stone blocks the next cell. If it crosses a compatible empty socket, it is captured there immediately and can no longer be pushed; incompatible sockets remain smooth floor and are crossed normally. The agent enters the stone’s former cell after a successful push. A push with no available sliding space fails visibly: the agent bumps the stone and the stone briefly shudders without changing the settled state.

Loose stones therefore have two roles without changing their rules: they are cargo and movable stopping surfaces. Walls establish initial braking points, but filled sockets permanently alter the board’s usable geometry. All important information—stone positions, compatibility, empty goals, and permanent obstacles—is readable from a single settled frame.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Build the brake:** A socket that initially cannot be approached precisely may become reachable after a different socket is filled beside its travel line. The newly raised captured stone visibly supplies the missing stopping surface, making delivery order a constructive tool rather than merely a restriction.

- **Park a temporary bumper:** One loose stone can stop another one cell short of itself, after which the parked stone may be approached from another side and moved away. This becomes necessary when no wall or completed goal occupies the required braking position, and it can be reused with either stone serving as the bumper.

- **Protect the pushing side:** A stone may stop in a useful row yet become unpushable in the needed direction because the agent cannot reach the cell behind it. Open floor around the resting stone makes this impasse legible, teaching players to judge both where a slide ends and whether its next launch position remains accessible.

- **Use harmless crossings:** A mismatched socket does not catch a passing stone, so interleaved routes can deliberately send stones across other goals before reaching their own. Persistent matching marks support safe experiments and later make apparently obstructive goal arrangements into usable transit lanes.

**Progression.** Foundational scenes separately demonstrate ordinary movement, full-distance sliding, collision stops, and unmistakable matching capture in spacious, recoverable settings. Early compositions require using a captured stone or a loose stone as a brake rather than aiming directly at a socket. Middle puzzles reuse those consequences while access around stones and pass-through mismatches change which approach direction is useful. Late puzzles combine temporary parking with permanent captured obstacles, making each delivery reshape several remaining routes. The final phase asks the player to infer a complete dependency order from visible stopping lines, approach cells, and compatibility without introducing another mechanic.

title: Freight Train
description:
A game about pushing lines of carts becoming difficult because touching carts permanently couple together.

A push propagates through every contiguous cart in the line. When compatible carts meet, they merge into a single visible train that thereafter moves as a unit. Building a longer train increases pushing reach but also makes turning, separating routes, and fitting through spaces impossible.

The game takes place on a compact top-down warehouse grid. A worker walks with `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT`; moving into a cart attempts to push it one cell. If other carts lie directly ahead, the push propagates through the line, but it succeeds only if every affected cart or coupled train can move into clear floor. A blocked push leaves the state unchanged and gives the obstructed edge a conspicuous red impact flash.

Each cart has a visible cargo emblem and hook-and-socket couplers on two opposite ends. Compatible coupler faces that touch lock permanently: the seam gains a heavy clasp and the joined carts share a continuous undercarriage, making the resulting train unmistakable. Pushing any member then translates the entire rigid train in the same direction without rotating it. Uncoupled carts may still transmit a push while touching, but hook-to-hook, socket-to-socket, and side contacts do not lock.

The primary objective is to place every cart on the delivery bay bearing its cargo emblem. A correctly occupied bay gains a bright border around that specific cart, so every remaining requirement is spatially visible. Walls define maneuvering chambers, narrow passages, and worker access; no other devices or hidden states are needed.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **A train becomes a long pushing tool.** Its visible far end can reach a cart when the worker cannot stand behind that cart, making intentional coupling necessary rather than merely hazardous.

- **Align before locking.** A long train cannot rotate or bend, so nearby corners and offset delivery bays visibly show why carts may need to be oriented, routed, or individually positioned before their compatible ends meet.

- **Exploit non-locking contact.** The exposed hook and socket shapes reveal that an incompatible end or a cart’s side can transmit force without permanent attachment, allowing a train to act as a ram and later move away; later puzzles require choosing which face makes contact.

- **Plan the whole translated footprint.** A push can fail because any part of a coupled train lacks destination space, even when its pushed end appears clear; wide staging areas can therefore be used to shift a train sideways before sending it through a narrow route.

**Progression:** Foundational scenes teach walking, propagated pushes, visible coupling, and matching bays in forgiving spaces where the demonstrated joins remain solvable. Early composition makes increased reach useful, then contrasts it with a delivery arrangement that cannot accept an accidentally lengthened train. The middle phase reuses coupler orientation and non-locking contact to move carts without absorbing them. Late warehouses combine restricted worker access, sideways staging, and goal patterns whose spacing determines which carts may safely couple. The final phase asks the player to construct the necessary trains in a workable order and route their rigid footprints to all bays without introducing any new rule.

title: Tumbling Blocks
description:
A game about pushing a cube becoming difficult because every move changes which face is exposed.

Each pushed cube rolls one cell and updates its visible top and side colors. A terminal activates only when the correct face touches its marked side, and the cube must ultimately occupy its dock in the required orientation. The route therefore determines both position and orientation.

The game uses an overhead grid containing a walking pusher, solid walls, tumbling cubes, wall-mounted terminals, and patterned docks. Every cube face has a unique color-and-symbol pairing. A cube shows its current top as a large central symbol, its four outward-facing sides as colored edge bands, and its underside as a small inset beside its shadow, making the complete orientation inspectable without memory.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the pusher one cell. Moving into a cube pushes it one cell if the destination is open; the cube visibly rolls in the same direction, and the pusher occupies its former cell. There is no pulling or separate interaction action.

Each terminal displays the face symbol it accepts on the side that the cube must touch. A successful contact permanently lights that terminal and leaves its accepted symbol glowing, while an incorrect contact produces a brief dull pulse; the cube’s visible contacting edge explains the failure. Docks remain traversable until occupied correctly and depict the required top and directional side faces. A level is complete when every required terminal is visibly lit and every cube rests on its matching dock in the displayed orientation.

Walls and other cubes block rolls. Failed movement makes the obstructed edge rock or flash, so no available direction appears silently inert. Early spaces avoid unrecoverable corners, while later hazards remain visually obvious rather than concealed.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Straight-roll cycles:** Repeated colors reveal that four rolls along one direction restore the full orientation, while two expose opposite faces. This lets players count usable lane lengths and decide where a turn must occur.

- **Turns do not commute:** Two open routes containing the same perpendicular rolls can reach the same cell with different faces exposed, plainly shown by the cube’s edge bands. Choosing turn order becomes necessary around walls and is later reused when approaching terminals from constrained sides.

- **Orientation loops:** A short closed route can return a cube to its previous cell while changing its orientation, which becomes evident beside a mismatched dock surrounded by open space. Such loops act as spatial orientation tools without introducing a rotate-in-place command.

- **Carry orientation beyond a terminal:** A lit terminal records success, but the cube continues from the contact with whatever orientation that roll produced. Later puzzles require satisfying several face contacts while shaping the remaining route so the final dock orientation is still attainable.

**Progression:** Foundational scenes separately establish pushing-and-rolling, readable face changes, and orientation-matched docking. Early composition introduces terminals and makes straight cycles and turn order necessary. Middle puzzles reuse those consequences in tighter approaches and reveal closed-route reorientation. Late puzzles combine multiple terminals, walls, and occasionally interacting cubes without changing the rolling rules. The final phase asks the player to choose one coherent route that performs all required contacts and ends in the exact dock orientation.

title: Crate Caps
description:
A game about stacking pieces becoming difficult because only completed stacks can support movement.

Small discs can be carried and dropped into visible pits. A single disc remains below floor level and is not walkable; a complete stack fills the pit and becomes solid terrain. Pieces must therefore be allocated between immediate crossings and later, more strategically important bridges.

The player guides a small courier across a tiled ruin to a clearly marked exit. Floor tiles are always walkable, while each circular pit occupies one tile and visibly holds two discs. Loose discs are finite, countable objects scattered on reachable floor, and the courier can carry only one at a time.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move one tile and set the courier’s visibly marked facing direction. `SPACE` acts on the faced adjacent cell: with empty hands it picks up a loose disc or retrieves the top disc from a pit, while carrying it deposits the disc into that pit. Loose discs and pits block entry, so the courier can face them without stepping onto them; a disc cannot be retrieved while the courier stands on the completed stack it would collapse.

A first disc settles visibly at the bottom of a pit, leaving a dark recess above it; the pit still blocks movement. A second disc creates a bright, flush cap continuous with the surrounding floor, making that tile walkable. Removing either disc from a completed stack immediately lowers its surface and makes it impassable again, so stacks are reversible terrain rather than permanently repaired ground.

The carried disc remains conspicuously above the courier, and every pit shows zero, one, or two visible layers in the settled frame. Attempts to walk into an incomplete pit produce a brief bump and rim pulse; an invalid `SPACE` action similarly pulses the faced object without changing state. The sole win condition is moving onto the visible exit tile.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Finish before spreading:** Two nearby half-filled pits consume all available pieces but create no foothold, while one completed pit advances the reachable frontier. Their visibly sunken tops make the failed allocation understandable and establish completion as the useful unit of terrain.

- **Preload a future approach:** A half-stack can be prepared from one bank even though it cannot yet be crossed, then completed later when the route reaches its opposite side with one carried disc. Persistent low discs make these advance deposits easy to track and useful in multiple branching routes.

- **Peel bridges from safe ground:** After stepping from a completed stack onto stable floor, the player can retrieve its cap and reuse it ahead, knowingly collapsing the old crossing. This turns apparently insufficient disc supplies into movable bridge material without adding another object or rule.

- **Preserve the working foothold:** In a chain of stacks, reclaiming the wrong cap removes the only tile from which another pit can be reached. The visible adjacency of courier, solid caps, and darkened incomplete pits supports reasoning backward from a safe bank and makes careful dismantling necessary.

**Progression:** Foundational scenes separately demonstrate carrying, the sunken first disc, the solid second disc, and safe retrieval with generous floor access. Early puzzles require concentrating discs and preloading pits rather than filling every visible gap greedily. Middle puzzles reuse bridge dismantling from opposite banks and across short branches containing additional discs. Late puzzles combine one-disc carrying, partial stacks, and reversible support so that immediate crossings compete visibly with more valuable future bridges. The final phase asks the player to construct, cross, and selectively dismantle an extended route using the same small set of objects and rules.

title: Beam Forge
description:
A game about joining blocks becoming difficult because larger pieces create access while losing flexibility.

Compatible bars merge when pushed together end-to-end. The resulting longer beam cannot be separated and occupies several cells as one object. Only beams of sufficient length can span marked chasms, but forging too early can leave the beam impossible to turn or position.

## Expanded Game Idea

The player guides a small forge worker through a gridded workshop, pushing rigid metal bars into position and ultimately reaching a clearly marked exit across one or more chasms. Bars occupy consecutive cells and have visible orientation, length, and stamped connector caps. When matching caps are pushed into direct end-to-end contact, the bars weld automatically; the joined seam remains visibly riveted, while the entire result thereafter moves and rotates as one inseparable beam.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the worker one cell. Moving into a bar pushes the entire bar or beam one cell in that direction if all required cells are clear; beams cannot be pulled. When the worker faces an exposed beam end, `SPACE` rotates the beam clockwise by a quarter-turn around that endpoint, provided its visible sweep is unobstructed. The worker’s facing is apparent from the sprite, and a blocked push or rotation highlights the obstructing cells; using `SPACE` without facing an endpoint produces a clear no-contact symbol rather than silence.

Walls and other beams block movement and rotation. Marked chasms have conspicuous paired support notches and ruler-like edge marks that communicate the span they require. A sufficiently long beam aligned across both supports seats into them, gains a bright walkway outline, and can then be crossed by the worker; shorter beams remain unsupported and visibly refuse the placement. Seated bridges no longer move, making their final position unambiguous. The exit is the sole win condition, so every bridge matters only insofar as it opens the visible route to that exit.

All relevant state is spatially persistent: occupied beam cells show length, end stamps show possible welds, welded seams show irreversible joins, and support brackets show completed bridges. Early workshops provide ample turning space and avoid misleading weld opportunities, allowing players to test pushing, rotation, and contact safely before irreversible assembly choices become consequential.

### Strategic discoveries

- **Turn before forging:** A short bar rotates through a small area while a long beam requires a visibly larger clear sweep, making pre-orientation necessary when the final beam would collide with nearby walls.
- **Choose the pivot end:** Rotating the same beam from its opposite exposed endpoint anchors a different cell, allowing it to enter spaces or align with supports that are unreachable from the first pivot.
- **Forge in place:** Instead of transporting a completed beam through a narrow workshop, separate bars can be staged near the chasm and joined by the final push, reusing welding as a positioning action.
- **Avoid needless overlength:** Extra segments can span the same gap but create obstructing overhang and consume turning room, so the player must sometimes reject an easy additional weld despite its apparent strength.

### Broad Progression

Foundational scenes establish translation, endpoint rotation, irreversible welding, bridge seating, and the exit objective in uncluttered spaces. Early composition makes pre-turning and deliberate forge location necessary. The middle phase reuses opposite-end pivots and in-place welding in contrasting wall and chasm arrangements. Late puzzles combine several assemblies whose work areas interfere, without adding unrelated devices. The final phase demands coordinated control of beam length, orientation, assembly location, and pivot access to forge the route to the exit.

title: Charge Relay
description:
A game about transferring charge becoming difficult because access depends on where the charge currently resides.

Only one adjacent token can hold the visibly glowing charge. Contact transfers charge from one token to another. Colored gates respond to the charged token’s type, while receptors activate only when charged tokens form a continuous visible alignment between source and endpoint.

The board is an arrangement of orthogonally touching relay tokens. Each token has an intrinsic type shown by both color and a bold central glyph. Exactly one token holds the transferable charge, distinguished by a bright corona; a directional input moves the corona to the touching token in that direction, darkens the former holder, and changes the active charge type to that of its new holder.

The corona also produces a live, nonpersistent conduction effect. Every token in an uninterrupted straight horizontal or vertical run through the holder becomes visibly energized with a bright inner stripe. Conduction stops at gaps and closed gates, and the entire stripe is recalculated after each transfer, so no token remains marked merely because it was visited. The unique corona identifies the charge holder, while the aligned stripes externalize which additional tokens are currently charged by it.

Colored gates occupy contacts between neighboring tokens. All gates matching the current holder’s type visibly open; other gates visibly close, blocking both transfer and conduction. Thus a transfer can pass through an open gate and then immediately change the gate pattern when the corona adopts the destination token’s type. A blocked attempt leaves the charge in place and makes the relevant gate and mismatched glyph pulse.

Each receptor has a clearly paired source terminal on the same row or column. It activates only when source and receptor are joined by one uninterrupted stripe of currently energized tokens; the receptor itself then shines and displays a complete line symbol. The primary objective is to leave every visible receptor active in the same settled frame, making success depend on the corona’s present location and type rather than its travel history.

**Controls:** `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` attempt to transfer the corona from its unique holder to the orthogonally touching token in that direction. If no token occupies that neighboring position or a gate blocks the contact, the corona remains in place and the attempted edge pulses while all legal neighboring contacts briefly brighten.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Landing changes access.** Passing a gate uses the departure token’s type, but landing gives the corona the destination glyph and visibly opens a different gate set; later routes require choosing destinations for the access they create, not merely for proximity.

- **Gates become directionally asymmetric.** A gate between differently typed tokens may be crossable from one side but closed on the return because the holder’s type changed. The two endpoint glyphs and settled gate state make this predictable and reusable in route planning.

- **Feed an alignment from its middle.** Any corona position within a straight run energizes the whole uninterrupted run, so an inaccessible source or receptor can be powered by approaching an interior token from the side. Visible stripes extending away from the holder reveal this alternative use.

- **Exploit intersections.** At a crossing of horizontal and vertical runs, one holder can energize both alignments, potentially satisfying multiple receptors at once. Later puzzles make reaching the correct intersection with the correct type necessary because a mismatched gate can sever one arm.

Foundational scenes establish adjacent transfer, type adoption, and one plainly visible live alignment with forgiving return routes. Early composition makes gate access change after landing and introduces predictable one-way crossings. The middle phase requires powering alignments from side approaches and reuses asymmetric access in different spatial arrangements. Late puzzles combine intersections with gates that also interrupt conduction, without adding another rule family. The final phase asks for a corona placement and type that simultaneously preserves every required source-to-receptor stripe.

title: Falling Scaffold
description:
A game about building supports becoming difficult because gravity resolves after every action.

Loose blocks fall until supported. The agent can carry and place lightweight braces beneath them, creating temporary platforms, stair patterns, or barriers. Removing or repositioning one support can trigger a cascade that opens one route while permanently blocking another.

The game is a side-view, cell-based construction puzzle. The primary objective is to guide the climber to a clearly visible exit hatch. Terrain is fixed, loose blocks are solid slabs, and braces are open lattice frames, making permanent ground, movable weight, and removable support immediately distinguishable. A carried brace remains visibly attached to the climber; every brace in the puzzle is therefore always accounted for.

`LEFT` and `RIGHT` walk, including stepping onto an adjacent one-cell ledge, and set the climber’s clearly visible horizontal facing. `UP` and `DOWN` climb or descend exposed brace lattice. `SPACE` picks up a brace directly in front of the climber or places the carried brace into the outlined empty cell directly ahead; authored layouts provide a side-access cell for every brace that must be manipulated. Invalid movement produces a visible bump, and an invalid `SPACE` target flashes without changing state.

After every input, loose blocks—and the climber if left over open space—fall vertically until supported by terrain, a brace, or another block. Braces remain fixed when loaded and may still be retrieved from an adjacent cell; doing so immediately releases everything they support. Blocks cannot be carried or pushed, so their final resting places are lasting consequences unless another brace can later be removed to release them again. The climber can stand on blocks and braces, allowing supported blocks to function as platforms or stairs, but a fallen block may also fill a shaft or seal a passage for the remainder of that attempt.

Cascades are shown briefly, but the settled frame contains the full state: block positions, loaded braces, reachable lattice, carried brace, climber, and exit. Early spaces provide broad catch floors and alternate access so experiments reveal gravity without causing obscure failures.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Height is a construction choice.** A brace visibly arrests a block at its own level, revealing that the same block can become a low barrier, a walking platform, or part of a staircase depending on where it is caught; later exits require choosing the useful resting height rather than merely preventing a fall.

- **Prepare the second landing first.** A supported block may have another visible brace or block lower in its fall line, so placing that catch before removing the upper support lets one slab descend in controlled stages. This becomes necessary when a full fall would seal the only approach needed to recover the brace.

- **Release order changes the structure.** When several offset blocks can land on one another, the first released block becomes support for the next, visibly changing subsequent stopping heights. The same set of slabs can therefore form either a climbable stair or an impassable wall, and later puzzles reuse this with release orders approached from different sides.

- **A barrier can be the route.** Dropping a slab may visibly close a lower corridor while raising its top into reach of a higher passage. Progress eventually requires accepting that opening the exit route can permanently sacrifice the route currently being used.

**Broad progression**

Foundational scenes establish carrying, supporting, climbing, and automatic settling in recoverable spaces. Early composition requires deliberate support height and pre-positioned catches. The middle phase reuses staged falls and release order where brace access comes from contrasting sides. Late puzzles combine stair construction with intentional corridor sealing, without adding new devices. The final phase asks the player to choreograph one coherent cascade whose resulting structure provides the only climb to the exit.

title: Twin Shadow
description:
A game about controlling two linked agents becoming difficult because every movement must work in two different spaces.

A second visible agent performs the horizontal mirror of every movement action. Either agent may be blocked while the other moves. Plates activate only while occupied, and the level ends when both agents simultaneously stand on their respective goals.

The screen shows two separate, equally prominent rooms divided by a clear mirror emblem. One agent inhabits each room, with a visually matching outlined goal in that same room. The rooms may have different wall arrangements, so corresponding movement does not produce corresponding positions.

**Controls:** `UP` and `DOWN` attempt to move both agents one cell in the same vertical direction. `LEFT` moves the first agent left and the second right; `RIGHT` does the reverse. These four directional actions are the complete control set. Each agent resolves obstruction independently: a wall, boundary, or closed gate keeps that agent still without canceling the other agent’s movement. A blocked agent visibly bumps against the obstacle and the obstructing edge flashes, making failed movement immediately understandable.

Pressure plates are floor cells that visibly depress and glow only while an agent stands on them. Each plate has an unmistakable symbol and visible connection to a gate bearing the same symbol, potentially in the other room. Occupying the plate retracts that gate; leaving it closes the gate again. Gates are barriers between cells rather than occupiable cells, so their current open or closed state is always unambiguous.

Goals glow while occupied, and a central two-part completion emblem illuminates one half for each occupied goal. This makes the simultaneous requirement persistent and spatially associated: reaching one goal is visibly useful but does not end the level.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Obstacles are clutches:** When one agent bumps while the other advances, the growing positional offset reveals that walls can deliberately decouple the pair. Later puzzles require using boundaries and gates to move one twin several cells without disturbing the other.

- **Alternate the anchored twin:** Different obstacle faces can hold each agent on different commands, allowing control to pass back and forth between them. Visible mismatches between an agent’s needed direction and its twin’s nearby wall suggest this technique, which becomes necessary for shaping both positions independently.

- **Hold while the other passes:** An agent on a plate can be kept there by issuing commands that its surrounding walls block, while those mirrored commands steer the other through the open gate. The depressed plate, open gate, and repeated harmless bumps clearly expose why the arrangement works.

- **Dock without undocking:** Placing one goal beside a useful blocking surface lets that agent remain on its glowing goal while the final commands align its twin. Later goal placements require recognizing which approach leaves the already-finished agent safely anchored rather than merely reaching goals in sequence.

Foundational scenes use open, recoverable spaces to establish mirrored horizontal movement, shared vertical movement, independent blocking, and simultaneous goals. Early composition makes intentional asymmetric blocking necessary rather than accidental. The middle phase introduces the visible plate-to-gate relationship, then reuses anchoring to maintain plate occupancy while navigating the opposite room. Late puzzles combine alternating anchors, cross-room gates, and goal docking without adding unrelated object families. The final phase demands coordinated use of both rooms’ geometry so that plate holding, selective movement, and simultaneous arrival form one continuous plan.

title: Floodline
description:
A game about outrunning water becoming difficult because every action advances a visible flood front.

Water spreads by one cell through connected empty space after each action. Flooded cells become impassable. The agent can construct solid dams that redirect the spread, but every dam also blocks movement and may cut off a route needed later.

**Game idea**

Floodline is a deterministic grid-based escape puzzle. The agent must reach a single raised exit while water expands orthogonally across open ground. Every movement or construction action gives the water one step of growth; if that growth reaches the agent, the contact is shown clearly and the attempt ends. A flooded exit or a dam-sealed route does not trigger an automatic loss: an unwinnable settled position remains visible for the player to recognize and externally reset.

Permanent rock forms the terrain. Water is solid blue, with pale foam marking every exposed edge of its current front. Constructed dams are thick, distinct barriers that block both the flood and the agent, while the exit is a prominent dry platform or doorway. The agent, water, rocks, dams, and exit are all visible at once, so the settled frame completely expresses the current state.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` attempt to move the agent one orthogonal cell. Eligible dry construction cells carry clear brackets. `SPACE` places a dam in the single adjacent bracket highlighted from the agent’s current position; authored layouts never expose more than one eligible bracket from the same cell. The new dam blocks the ensuing spread. A blocked move or invalid `SPACE` press produces an immediate bump or red rejection mark and still spends the action, visibly advancing the flood in accordance with the central rule.

Water has no hidden speed or branching choice: after each action, it occupies every open cell one orthogonal step beyond its existing front unless rock or a dam intervenes. Dams never move or disappear. Early spaces provide enough distance and alternate routes for the player to observe this behavior safely, including how a barrier can protect one area while making another inaccessible.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Chokepoint leverage.** Foam pressing against one dam while a large region beyond remains dry reveals that sealing a narrow neck prevents many later expansions. This becomes necessary when the construction action costs less time than the route it protects.

- **Detour multiplication.** A dam placed beside existing rock can make the flood travel around a long bend rather than merely losing one cell of progress; the redirected front remains visibly traceable. Later puzzles require creating such detours where no opening can be sealed outright.

- **Seal behind yourself.** Crossing a bottleneck before filling its adjacent construction cell lets the agent sacrifice the route only after using it. The stranded foam on the far side demonstrates the technique, which can be reused when choosing among several crossings.

- **Barrier economy.** A long wall is often self-defeating because every segment advances the flood, while a carefully selected single dam may redirect an entire branch. Visible partial walls overtaken during experimentation teach the need to judge each dam by the delay it creates, not its size.

**Progression**

Foundational scenes establish the exit, one-step flood growth, concrete contact loss, and the shared impassability of water and dams. Early composition makes chokepoint leverage and the action cost of construction necessary. The middle phase contrasts complete seals with barriers that force long detours, then requires sealing routes after crossing them. Late puzzles combine branching flood fronts with several tempting construction sites, demanding economical choices among already understood consequences. The final phase integrates crossing order, rear seals, and redirection into one escape governed entirely by the flood-and-dam system.

title: Painted Footprints
description:
A game about painting routes becoming difficult because objects can travel only over matching floor.

The agent carries one visible paint pot and paints cells while moving. Colored parcels may be pushed only across floor matching their color. The player paints transport lanes, changes paint pots at stations, and must avoid making a route suitable for one parcel but unusable for another.

The game is a compact grid puzzle about a courier preparing and continually altering parcel routes. The directional controls move the courier one cell; entering an empty paintable cell coats it with the carried pot’s color, replacing any previous paint. The courier may walk over any floor, but moving directly into a parcel attempts to push it: the push succeeds only if the parcel’s destination cell is already painted with its color and is unobstructed. After a successful push, the courier enters and paints the parcel’s vacated cell, so pushing while carrying another color visibly converts the route behind the parcel.

Walking onto a fixed paint station automatically exchanges the carried pot for that station’s displayed color. Stations have an unmistakable raised, striped appearance and cannot themselves be painted or occupied by parcels. Walls and board edges simply block movement. The objective is to place every parcel on a pad bearing its matching color and symbol; each occupied correct pad gains a persistent bright border, and the level ends when all pads are simultaneously satisfied.

Colors are reinforced with patterns shared by pots, paint, parcels, stations, and pads. The carried pot is drawn prominently on the courier, while exposed floor around a parcel keeps its supporting paint readable. A failed push makes the parcel shudder and highlights the mismatched destination cell, whose settled color already explains the failure; collisions with walls receive a similarly immediate bump response.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Travel is editing:** A shortcut across a prepared lane leaves an obvious trail of the carried color and may ruin it for its parcel. Later puzzles require choosing courier approaches that paint useful cells rather than casually crossing completed lanes.

- **Paint first, push second:** A parcel cannot enter an unprepared cell, and finishing a lane often leaves the courier on the parcel’s front side. Visible side access and the courier’s final position suggest preparing the route, circling around, and only then pushing from behind.

- **Brushback conversion:** Pushing a parcel while carrying another color replaces each vacated tile with that second color. This turns one parcel’s completed journey into a prepared lane for a following parcel, making pot choice during transport strategically important rather than cosmetic.

- **Time-shared crossings:** A narrow intersection cannot serve differently colored parcels at once, but it can be repainted after one parcel passes. Parcel positions, exposed crossing color, and remaining pad symbols reveal which transport order preserves access for the required repaint.

Foundational scenes separately establish footprint painting, matching-floor pushes, visible delivery pads, and automatic pot changes, using generous circulation space so experiments are recoverable. Early composition makes courier positioning and the destructive effect of walking across prepared paint necessary. The middle phase reuses those facts in shared corridors, then reveals deliberate brushback conversion as a way to prepare a second shipment. Late puzzles combine route preparation, parcel order, station access, and repaintable intersections without introducing unrelated devices. The final phase asks the player to orchestrate several parcels through overlapping lanes whose colors must change at the right moments.

title: Sand Channels
description:
A game about filling terrain becoming difficult because poured material continues spreading after every move.

Sand enters visible channels and advances through one connected cell per action. Completely filled basins become walkable, while partially filled channels remain blocked. Filling is permanent, so the player must control branching flows and avoid exhausting sand in irrelevant basins.

**Game idea**

The player guides a surveyor across dry stone toward a clearly marked exit. Between safe areas lie outlined channel basins, a finite sand hopper, and occasional fork-shaped diverters. Each basin contains several visibly separated cells; loose sand occupying only part of its outline remains impassable, while filling its final cell compacts the whole basin into a flat, unmistakably walkable surface.

Arrow keys move the surveyor one cell. Every successful step also releases exactly one visible unit from the hopper, filling the next empty channel cell along the route selected by the diverters. `SPACE` turns the single adjacent, highlighted diverter; its physical paddle rotates to point toward the chosen branch. A blocked movement produces a bump without releasing sand, while an unavailable `SPACE` action visibly shakes the surveyor’s tool rather than failing silently.

The seed’s reference to a “connected cell” could otherwise require inferring global connectivity. The smallest faithful clarification is that channel beds carry engraved flow marks, every fork has a persistent paddle orientation, and the cell due to receive the next unit displays a distinct leading ridge of loose sand. Turning a diverter immediately relocates that ridge, so the settled frame always reveals the current route, remaining supply, basin completion, and next local consequence.

The goal is simply to step onto the exit. Sand is not separately scored: it matters because completing selected basins creates the only useful crossings, while sending too much into side basins can leave every remaining route visibly incomplete.

**Strategic discoveries**

- **Footsteps are the flow clock.** The hopper loses a unit and the leading ridge advances whenever the surveyor walks, making it discoverable that longer dry-land routes may feed the wrong branch before the player reaches its diverter; later puzzles require positioning near a fork before taking additional steps.

- **Completion beats distribution.** Two half-filled basins remain two barriers, whereas concentrating the same visible supply can create one crossing. Early tempting forks expose this contrast, and later situations reuse it when the player must decide which crossing must become usable first.

- **A filled basin is both bridge and conduit.** Once compacted, later sand passes through that basin toward the next empty cell, visibly moving the leading ridge beyond it. This makes completing an upstream basin useful for opening access and for feeding a farther basin, but only if its downstream diverter is prepared.

- **Build a shorter clock path.** Filling a nearby basin may initially seem indirect, yet its new walkable surface can shorten the surveyor’s route to another diverter, saving several automatic releases. Later puzzles require recognizing which sand-built shortcut reduces movement enough to prevent an irrelevant basin from consuming the remaining supply.

**Progression**

Foundational scenes use generous hoppers and obvious single routes to establish movement-triggered spreading, permanent filling, and basin completion. Early composition introduces forks where concentrating flow and reaching a diverter in time become necessary. The middle phase contrasts using a basin as an immediate crossing with completing it to carry flow farther downstream. Late challenges combine route length, diverter preparation, and sand-built shortcuts without adding unrelated devices. The final phase asks the player to shape one limited flow network into both the walkable route and the means of delivering sand to its remaining gaps.

title: Rotating Maze
description:
A game about rotating arrows becoming difficult because both the agent and cargo obey the resulting routes.

The agent can rotate visible arrow tiles. Entering an arrow deflects the agent, while pushed or launched balls continue along the arrow network until stopped. A route that delivers the ball may leave the agent unable to reach the final exit unless junctions are prepared in the correct sequence.

**Game idea**

A turn-based grid maze contains an agent, solid walls, ordinary floor, rotatable arrow tiles, cargo balls, circular cargo bays, and an exit. The objective is to launch every ball into a bay, visibly opening the exit, and then route the agent into that exit. Filled bays remain occupied and illuminated, while the exit’s ball-shaped lock visibly changes to an open doorway, making every remaining requirement readable from the settled frame.

`UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, and `RIGHT` move the agent one cell and set its visibly indicated facing direction. Moving into a ball pushes and launches it if the cell beyond is free. `SPACE` rotates the arrow directly in front of the agent clockwise; rotatable arrows have a distinct rim, and if none is in reach the agent’s facing marker pulses against the blocked cell.

When the agent enters an arrow tile, that arrow immediately ejects it one cell in the arrow’s direction. Entering another arrow continues the chain, while reaching ordinary floor ends the forced movement. A launched ball keeps traveling straight across floor, turns whenever it crosses an arrow, and stops immediately before a wall, another ball, or another solid obstruction; reaching a bay captures it. Inputs occur only after all movement has settled, so there is no hidden momentum or timing state.
